stem: In the epidemiology of pediatric urinary tract infections, how does the prevalence change between genders as a child ages?

options.text: UTIs are more common in girls during the first year, but boys take over after $12$ months.
UTIs are more common in boys during the first $6$ to $12$ months, then more common in girls.
Boys and girls have equal prevalence until the age of seven, at which point girls reach $8\%$.
Girls are more likely to have a UTI at every stage of development starting from birth.

explanation: Infant boys have a higher incidence of UTIs in the first year, but after this window, the prevalence in girls becomes significantly higher.
rationale: Consider which gender has a higher incidence specifically during the neonatal and early infancy period.

optionExplanations.A: While girls generally have higher rates throughout childhood, the first year of life is the only period where boys show a higher prevalence.
optionExplanations.B: Infant boys have a higher incidence of UTIs in the first year, but after this window, the prevalence in girls becomes significantly higher.
optionExplanations.C: Statistical data shows distinct gender differences well before age seven, with girls reaching $8\%$ and boys reaching $2\%$ cumulative incidence by that age.
optionExplanations.D: This ignores the specific trend where boys actually have a higher incidence during the first $6$ to $12$ months of life.

source.hint: Consider which gender has a higher incidence specifically during the neonatal and early infancy period.
